title: Who pays for the AI buildout? $10 trillion, Hyperion and Dutch pensions
summary: As tech stocks enter a bear market, we take apart Van Nieuwerburgh's anatomy of the AI buildout: from $8.2 billion per campus and Meta's 90%-debt Hyperion structure to the $3.7 trillion in annual revenue the buildout needs to earn back. Then: what a correction means for Dutch pension funds, and how to turn the paper's measurement gap into an extraction project.
shownotes:
This week's sell-off: Nasdaq 100 down 10.4%, Nvidia down 14% on an SEC review, Anthropic down 9.1% after its debut
The rack arithmetic: a 200 MW campus costs about $8.2bn, 68% of it IT equipment with a six-year life
From pipeline to scenario: 566 GW reported, about 183 GW built by 2032, $10.3 trillion (NBER version: nearly $9 trillion), 3.6% of GDP, bigger than the railroads
Why financing moves off balance sheet: hyperscaler capex exceeds operating cash flow in 2026; labs borrow the hyperscalers' credit rating
Meta's Hyperion and the Beignet vehicle: 90% debt, DSCR 1.12x, four-year leases plus a residual value guarantee, over $5bn extra interest for an asset-light look
The revenue requirement: about $3.7 trillion a year by 2032, $5.5 to $8.8 per GPU-hour depending on utilisation and IT life
Where losses land: tenant concentration, obsolescence, execution, circular financing; Clouds of Credit's $16.8 trillion low-productivity scenario
Dutch exposure: DNB's ESB scenario, pension funds' roughly 45% of listed equity in tech, and DNB's AI adoption study
Takeaways: rebuild Appendix D as a model, build a cited extraction pipeline for off-balance-sheet commitments, keep model choice portable
